catalog_quote: 1.4 WORD BOUNDARIES. To determine word boundaries in Maleu three criteria are employed: the stress pattern on compounds, the occurrence of known isolated words in larger forms, and the occurrence of clitics. 1.4.1 STRESS PATTERN ON COMPOUNDS. When certain words are compounded, stress shifts to the penultimate syllable and in some cases vowels also change to effect vowel harmony. The preference in spelling is to follow the phonological form. 'avo 'not' + ta becomes a'vota 'not yet'; 'avo 'not' + la becomes a'vola 'and so'; 'tia 'one' + 'tia 'one' becomes ti'atia [ti'atya] 'one by one'; na-'roro 'NM-road' + tne 'his/her.mother' becomes naro'rotne 'the big road'; na-'vola 'NM-man' + tia 'one' becomes navo'latia [nabo'latya] 'one man'; na-'vola 'NM-man' + lua 'two' becomes navo'lalua [nabo'lalwa] 'two men'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Haywood (Maleu/Lolo dialect) never states a general stress rule; his only stress section concerns compounds, but every stress-marked form he gives, simplex and compound, carries stress on the penultimate syllable ('avo, 'ria, 'ire, 'lua, na-'roro, na-'vola; a'vota, ti'atia, naro'rotne, navo'latia, navo'lalua, er'elua), i.e. stress is recomputed on the penult of the whole compound. Goulden (Kilenge dialect), in a passing remark in the morphosyntax section, asserts 'regular antepenultimate stress' and uses it to explain why the noun prefix na- is not degeminated in naa-pe 'paddle'. The two first-hand descriptions of the two dialects therefore point to penultimate (Haywood, implicit, 13 consistent forms) vs antepenultimate (Goulden, explicit, one example); neither gives a full rule or a data set on simplex words.
new_statements.exceptions: Haywood: compounding causes stress to 'shift' to the penult of the compound, sometimes with vowel changes (vowel harmony); 'ire 'they' + 'lua 'two' has three variant forms er'elua / er'emua / er'elmua. Goulden: the na- prefix 'can take' the stress (naa-pe), which he treats as regular antepenultimate stress; no other exceptions. Friederici 1912 (Bariai section, p. ~188) remarks in general that in Barriai 'wie in allen mir bekannt gewordenen melanesischen Sprachen' accent lacks the significance and fixedness it has in German — not specific to Kilenge.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: Haywood uses the stress pattern as one of three criteria for word boundaries (section 1.4), so stress is a property of the phonological word, including compounds; forms are citation/elicited forms with IPA-style stress marks before the stressed syllable. Goulden's remark concerns the prefixed noun (na- + root). No phrase-level or intonation statements in either source.
new_statements.identity_note: Haywood 1996 describes the Maleu (= Lolo) dialect (Glottolog dialect male1290), data from Pototpua village 1974-77; Goulden 1996 calls the language 'Kilenge' after the dialect his data come from (Glottolog kile1242; one Kilenge speaker in a Lusi village 1982 plus Jill Grant's notes). Ross's 1996 volume introduction confirms Goulden's 'Kilenge' and Haywood's 'Maleu' are the same language (language-level male1289). The earlier scan's 'SIL PNG (Data Papers)' attribution is wrong: Haywood 1996 is a Pacific Linguistics C-135 chapter (ANU), and Goulden 1996 is in the same volume.
